issues.legal_issue: Intentionally inflicting a bodily injury sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death constitutes murder when the elements of the applicable murder clause are established.
material_facts: The accused inflicted three sharp-edged injuries on the victim.
After the first injury caused the victim to fall, the accused inflicted two further injuries while the victim was on the ground.
The third injury cut the victim’s neck and was found sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The court inferred that the accused intended to inflict the two injuries delivered after the victim had fallen.
issues.conclusion: The intentional infliction of the fatal injury, which was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, brought the offence within clause thirdly of Section 300 IPC and constituted murder.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 299 and 300 clause thirdly IPC, culpable homicide is murder where the accused intends to inflict the bodily injury actually found and that injury is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. Applying Virsa Singh v. State of Punjab, AIR 1958 SC 465, the court treats the existence and nature of the injury, the intention to inflict that injury, and its objective sufficiency to cause death as distinct matters. The intention is inferred from all the circumstances, including the location and nature of the injury, the weapon, and the force used. Death need not be inevitable: a very high probability of death is sufficient; where the probability is lower, the offence is culpable homicide not amounting to murder. Rajwant Singh v. State of Kerala, AIR 1966 SC 1844, was also relied on.

predicates.murder_conviction_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal against a conviction for murder.
predicates.bodily_injury_intentionally_inflicted: The accused intentionally inflicted the bodily injury found on the victim, as inferred from the circumstances of the attack.
predicates.injury_sufficient_in_ordinary_course_to_: The bodily injury inflicted was sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.

issues.definition: When an appeal against a murder conviction concerns an intentionally inflicted injury that is sufficient in the ordinary course to cause death, the rule identifies the offence as murder.

issues.legal_issue: The sudden-fight exception does not apply when the accused takes undue advantage or acts cruelly or unusually, even if the fatal attack follows a sudden quarrel without premeditation.
material_facts: The accused used a sharp-edged deadly weapon against a victim who was unarmed and had caused no injury to the accused.
The first blow caused the victim to fall, but the accused continued to inflict two more blows while the victim lay on the ground.
The third blow inflicted on the fallen victim was fatal.
The accused relied on the sudden quarrel and heat of passion to claim the benefit of the exception.
issues.conclusion: The accused took undue advantage and acted cruelly; the sudden-fight exception did not apply, and the offence remained murder.
issues.legal_principle: Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC requires that the act be committed without premeditation in a sudden fight, in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting cruelly or unusually. The court relied on Pandurang Narayan Jawalekar v. State of Maharashtra, [1979] 1 SCC 132. Whether the offender took undue advantage depends on the weapons used, the parties’ relative ability to defend themselves, and the manner of the attack; using a deadly weapon against an unarmed person and continuing to attack a fallen victim can establish undue advantage and cruel conduct.
